sense: fill with a feeling or the will to act

terms.gloss: put into, inspire (a feeling in someone)
terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, transitive; the feeling in the accusative, the person in the dative
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “to bring into, inspire, infuse”. Its first sense is to throw in or on; with a feeling it says what the feeling is: spem injicere, inspire hope; metum injicere, inspire fear.

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation, transitive; ad + acc. or the abl.
evidence: Cic. Fam. 1.7.9: ā pueritiā īnflammātus ad glōriam (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Lael. 86: īnflammārī cupiditāte honōrum (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Inspire as setting someone on fire for something; literally, to set alight.

evidence: Cic. N.D. 2.167: nēmō vir magnus sine aliquō afflātū dīvīnō umquam fuit (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: A breath or blast; in Cicero the breath of a god in a great man or an orator.

terms.gloss: breathe into; inspire (a feeling); in Christian Latin, inspire
terms.register: vōx plērumque poētica: Verg.; in ōrātiōne solūtā post Augustum (Quint., Curt.)
evidence: Verg. A. 6.12: magnam mentem animumque (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Poetic and post-Augustan (Lewis & Short); the word of the Vulgate for inspiration by the Holy Spirit, and so of church life.

phrases.latin: nēmō vir magnus sine aliquō afflātū dīvīnō umquam fuit
phrases.english: no man was ever great without some divine inspiration

sources: Lewis & Short: inicio · Lewis & Short: inflammo · Lewis & Short: afflatus · Lewis & Short: inspiro
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
